summary: This standards-track RFC extends SIIT-DC with a dual translation mode. It lets applications, protocols or nodes that cannot work with IPv6 or with NAT keep operating correctly, by adding a second translation step on the data center side.

plainLanguage.summary: Some old machines only understand the old language. This adds a second translator inside so even they can keep working.

subtitle: Adds an Edge Relay so IPv4-only software can run inside an IPv6-only data center with its real IPv4 addresses intact.

tldr.problem: SIIT-DC lets IPv4-only users reach IPv6-only services, but it works poorly or not at all for protocols that break under NAT, nodes that cannot use IPv6, and software that assumes IPv4 is available.
tldr.mechanism: A new component, the SIIT-DC Edge Relay (ER), sits near the IPv4-only node or application and reverses the translation done by the Border Relay (BR), so the node sees native-looking IPv4 with the original addresses.
tldr.outcome: IPv4-only applications get virtual IPv4 connectivity with end-to-end address transparency in an otherwise IPv6-only network. The document is an extension to RFC 7755 and assumes the reader knows it.

sections.title: Why SIIT-DC Needs an Edge Relay
sections.content:
RFC 7755 describes SIIT-DC, an architecture in which IPv4-only users reach IPv6-only services through a stateless translator called the SIIT-DC Border Relay (BR). RFC 7756 starts from the cases where that approach works poorly or not at all.

  • Application protocols that do not support NAT, because they need end-to-end transparency of IP addresses.
  • Nodes that cannot connect to IPv6 networks at all, or can only do so if they also get IPv4 connectivity.
  • Application software that uses legacy IPv4-only APIs or assumes IPv4 is available.

The fix is a second translator, the Edge Relay (ER). It reverses the IPv4-to-IPv6 translation the BR made, and hands the result to the node or application as native IPv4. Traffic in the other direction is translated to IPv6, sent to the BR, and translated back for the IPv4 client.
sections.plainLanguage: Some programs only know the old way of talking. The Edge Relay stands next to them and translates everything back to the old way, so they keep working.

sections.title: The Key Building Blocks
sections.content:
The document leans on a handful of terms.

  • Border Relay (BR): performs stateless IPv4/IPv6 translation, and MUST follow RFC 6145 and RFC 7757.
  • Edge Relay (ER): provides native IPv4 to IPv4-only devices or software. It works like a BR but sits close to the IPv4-only component rather than on the outer border of the Internet Data Center (IDC).
  • IPv4 Service Address and IPv6 Service Address: a pair of addresses for the same node or service, coupled by an Explicit Address Mapping (EAM) configured in the BR or ER.
  • Translation prefix: an IPv6 prefix into which the whole IPv4 address space is mapped under RFC 6052. A relay adds or removes it from addresses, unless an EAM exists for that address.
sections.plainLanguage: Each machine gets two names, an old-style one and a new-style one, and a list says which goes with which. The translators use that list to swap names.

sections.title: How the Edge Relay Works
sections.content:
An ER is at its core an implementation of the stateless translation algorithm of RFC 6145 that supports EAMs from RFC 7757. A packet from the IPv4 Internet to an IPv4 Service Address is first translated to IPv6 by the BR. It is then forwarded to the ER that owns the matching IPv6 Service Address, and the ER translates it back to IPv4 for the node. The reverse direction uses exactly the same translations in reverse.

An ER may handle any number of service addresses. Every EAM in the BR that involves addresses handled by an ER MUST also be present in that ER's configuration.

There are two kinds of ER, chosen per service or per node, and any number of each may coexist:

  • Node-based: a software function inside an otherwise IPv6-only node. It may create a virtual network adapter that holds the IPv4 Service Address and a default IPv4 route, so applications can use IPv4-only calls such as AF_INET sockets. The RFC compares this to the Bump-in-the-Stack approach of RFC 6535, without an Extension Name Resolver.
  • Network-based: the ER provides an isolated IPv4 network segment and acts as the default IPv4 router for the nodes on it. Each node MUST acquire an IPv4 Service Address and assign it to a local interface.

In both cases native IPv6 can be offered at the same time, which makes dual-stack operation possible if the application supports it. The ER needs a dedicated IPv6 Service Address for each IPv4 Service Address, and the IPv6 network MUST forward traffic for those addresses to the node, for example by assigning them as secondary IPv6 addresses so the upstream router learns them through Neighbor Discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: The translator can live inside the computer like a built-in dictionary, or in a small room next to it that all the old-style computers talk through.

sections.title: Network-Based Layouts
sections.content:
A basic network-based ER creates an IPv4-only segment between itself and the nodes it serves. That is fine for nodes with no IPv6 support, but it takes away IPv6 from dual-stack nodes. The RFC RECOMMENDS a node-based ER for dual-stack nodes, but notes it may not exist for every node. If the application protocol does not work in a NAT environment, standard SIIT-DC cannot be used either, which leaves a network-based ER as the only solution. Two layouts keep IPv6 alive:

  • ER on a stick: the ER's IPv4 and IPv6 interfaces sit on the same network segment (or one dual-stacked interface is used). Native IPv6 bypasses the ER, while IPv4 goes to the ER as the default IPv4 router. The ER can attract inbound traffic for the IPv6 Service Addresses by answering the upstream router's Neighbor Discovery messages.
  • ER that bridges IPv6 packets: the ER transparently bridges IPv6 frames between its upstream and downstream interfaces, and intercepts packets for IPv6 Service Addresses to translate them. The downstream segment becomes dual stacked.

Appendix A gives two ways to address the IPv4 side. A subnet that encloses the IPv4 Service Addresses, with the ER handing them out by DHCPv4, is simple but can break contact with other services in the same prefix, because nodes try to resolve them with ARP instead of sending them to the ER. A private unrouted IPv4 network avoids that overlap, but rules out using DHCPv4 for the service addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: If the old-style computer also speaks the new language, you do not want to cut that off. So the translator is placed so that new-style messages walk straight past it and only old-style ones get translated.

sections.title: MTU and Fragmentation Tuning
sections.content:
The IPv6 Path MTU between the ER and the BR will usually be larger than the 1280-byte default in RFC 6145, since both sit inside one administrative domain. The RFC RECOMMENDS raising the ER's configured IPv6 Path MTU, and using identical values on the ER and the BR.

To avoid IPv6 fragmentation, an ER SHOULD make the IPv4 MTU used by applications equal to the configured IPv6 Path MTU minus 20, so a maximum-sized IPv4 packet fits in an unfragmented IPv6 packet. A node-based ER can set this on its virtual adapter. A network-based ER can advertise it with the DHCPv4 Interface MTU option.

The IPv4 Identification value is lost in translation if IPv6 Atomic Fragments are disabled. Enabling them carries it end to end, but must be enabled on both the BR and the ER to work in both directions. The RFC notes that few application protocols use this field apart from certain diagnostic tools.
sections.plainLanguage: Translated letters need a slightly bigger envelope. So the translator tells everyone to write a bit less on each page, and nothing has to be cut in half.

sections.title: Talking Inside the Data Center
sections.content:
An IPv4-only node behind an ER may need to reach other services inside the IDC. The RFC describes two ways.

Hairpinning by the BR. If the BR supports hairpinning (RFC 7757), the target service is simply made available through SIIT-DC in the normal way, with an EAM in the BR. The ER translates the packet by inserting the translation prefix, the BR hairpins it back toward the target's IPv6 Service Address, and return traffic is hairpinned the same way. If the target is behind another ER, a third translation happens there.

Additional EAMs in the ER. If the BR cannot hairpin, or hairpinning is not wanted, the ER can be given extra EAMs for each service it must reach. Traffic then follows the direct path through the IPv6 network, avoiding the BR, which might give better latency. A target behind another ER MUST also be provisioned with an EAM for the origin, or it cannot translate the source address.

If the nodes do not need the public IPv4 Internet, private addresses (RFC 1918) can serve as their IPv4 Service Addresses, saving the operator's public addresses. For a native IPv6 target, the address could come from the IPv4 Service Continuity Prefix of RFC 7335.
sections.plainLanguage: Two old-style computers in the same building still talk through translators. They can send mail via the main post office at the gate, or use a shortcut straight between their translators.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Two risks are specific to the ER. First, if the ER gets an IPv4 packet from a source it has no EAM for, it rewrites both addresses using the translation prefix, and after the BR reverses it the IPv4 packet leaves with a spoofed source address. The ER SHOULD therefore apply ingress filtering (RFC 2827) on its IPv4 interface so such packets are dropped at once.

Second, an IPv6 packet whose source and destination are both one of the ER's own IPv6 Service Addresses would look locally generated to the IPv4-only application, which could trust it as coming from itself. The ER SHOULD discard received IPv6 packets whose source equals one of its local IPv6 Service Addresses, or equals one of its local IPv4 Service Addresses after translation. General SIIT-DC concerns are in RFC 7755.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not let a stranger copy your name tag and pretend to be you. The translator checks name tags at the door and turns away anyone wearing one that looks like its own.
